Project overview

I wanted to use public HIV estimates to go beyond comparing the number of new infections across countries. Our World in Data already has useful charts for those trends. For this project, I focused on three questions that require additional calculations or combining indicators: how countries’ infection estimates changed after their observed peaks, whether maternal ART coverage is associated with pediatric HIV outcomes in later years, and whether conclusions about epidemic progress differ when choosing UNAIDS or IHME estimates collected from 1990-2016 and their reported uncertainty.

I used Kenya, South Africa, and Uganda as case studies. These are estimated population-level indicators, not individual patient records. My analyses describe patterns and associations; they do not establish that a particular intervention caused a change in infections.

Data and preparation

I downloaded the underlying indicators from Our World in Data and checked the original source, units, age group, year coverage, and country labels. Each input file has one row per country and year. I did not average real-world duplicate country-year records: the analysis stops if it finds duplicates so I can investigate them. Missing observations are retained where needed for a data-quality audit, rather than silently filled in.

I used separate files for UNAIDS incidence, IHME incidence, maternal ART coverage, and pediatric infections. Before comparing UNAIDS and IHME, I checked that both incidence files refer to the same age group and annual count measure. The maternal ART variable is a percentage, while pediatric infections are annual counts. These are different units and should not be interpreted as directly comparable quantities.

Analysis 1: Post-peak trajectories

Question: After each country’s highest observed annual infection estimate, how did subsequent estimates change relative to that peak?

I identified each country’s peak from the available UNAIDS series. I then expressed later estimates as a percentage of that country’s peak and aligned countries by years since peak. This allows me to compare relative trajectories even when peak years and absolute infection counts differ. It does not adjust for population size, and an observed peak can change if the dataset is updated.

print(p_peak)

knitr::kable(post_peak_summary, digits = 1,
             caption = 'Observed peaks and number of post-peak observations')
Observed peaks and number of post-peak observations
country peak_year peak_infections last_year n_observed
Kenya 1992 250000 2025 34
South Africa 1999 530000 2025 27
Uganda 1990 110000 2025 36

Interpretation: I will describe the direction and relative size of each country’s post-peak change after reviewing the output. I will not infer the reasons for those changes from this chart alone.

Analysis 2: Maternal ART and pediatric HIV

Question: Is higher ART coverage among pregnant women living with HIV associated with fewer estimated pediatric HIV infections in the same year or in later years?

I matched maternal ART coverage in year t to pediatric HIV infections in year t + L, where L is a lag of zero to three years. The two-year lag is the main example, and the other lags are sensitivity checks. I chose this range to explore whether results depend on timing; it is not a validated biological delay, and the data cannot identify when individual transmissions occurred.

I compare a simple regression with a model that also includes country indicators and a linear outcome-year trend, when enough complete observations are available. I use log1p() on pediatric infection counts so the outcome can include zeros. The models describe ecological associations, not causal effects. They also cannot fully account for changes in testing, birth rates, access to care, or other interventions.

Analysis 3: Source sensitivity and estimation uncertainty (1990–2016)

Research question: Do UNAIDS and IHME estimates lead to consistent conclusions about HIV epidemic progress in Kenya, South Africa, and Uganda from 1990–2016, and how does estimation uncertainty affect our confidence in those conclusions?

I compared the same all-age, both-sex annual counts of new HIV infections from the UNAIDS 2026 estimates workbook and IHME exports. I restricted both sources to 1990–2016, the common period covered by the downloaded files. I combined the three IHME country CSVs in R, and retained the estimate, lower bound, and upper bound from each source. The analysis requires matching country and calendar year; it does not impute missing estimates. Because the two organizations use different estimation methods, differences do not establish which source is correct.

Stage 1: Comparing epidemic progress

For each source and country, I identified the year with the largest estimated number of new infections within 1990–2016. I then calculated the percentage change from that source-specific peak to 2016 and the average annual change in estimated infection counts over the same interval. The average annual change is an endpoint-based descriptive measure, not a regression slope. When two years have equal peak estimates, the earlier year is selected. If a peak occurs in 2016, post-peak change is undefined rather than reported as zero.

Interpretation to complete after running the analysis: Describe whether peak years and subsequent changes differ by source, and whether a country’s apparent progress changes when using a different source. These are estimated counts, not population-standardized incidence rates.

Stage 2: Evaluating estimation uncertainty

I compared the reported lower and upper bounds for each matched year and calculated how often the two reported intervals overlap. I also recorded whether either source’s point estimate falls inside the other source’s interval, and calculated each interval’s width relative to its point estimate. These summaries describe the uncertainty reported for individual annual estimates. Interval overlap is not a hypothesis test, and the two sources may use different uncertainty methods or coverage conventions.

knitr::kable(uncertainty, digits=1,
             caption='Descriptive uncertainty comparisons across matched years')
Descriptive uncertainty comparisons across matched years
country n_interval_pairs n_overlap pct_overlap n_unaids_inside_ihme n_ihme_inside_unaids median_unaids_width_pct median_ihme_width_pct
Kenya 27 19 70.4 14 6 25.0 38.6
South Africa 27 23 85.2 10 17 65.9 35.8
Uganda 27 15 55.6 11 4 20.0 61.6 
print(p_intervals)

Interpretation to complete after running the analysis: Identify whether the estimates are often separated or accompanied by wide intervals. Avoid saying that overlapping intervals prove agreement or that non-overlap identifies the more accurate source.

Stage 3: Testing sensitivity of conclusions

I repeated the same calculations using each source separately. I then compared peak years, the direction and magnitude of peak-to-2016 change, and country rankings by percentage decline. This asks whether the choice of source changes a substantive conclusion rather than merely whether point estimates differ.

Kenya 3 1 FALSE
South Africa 1 2 FALSE
Uganda 2 3 FALSE 
print(p_sensitivity)

To explore how sensitive the direction of change is to reported endpoint ranges, I also calculated an illustrative stress test: the smallest and largest percentage changes obtained by combining the reported bounds at the selected peak year and in 2016. The peak year is held fixed. These extremes are not joint probability intervals and must not be presented as confidence or uncertainty intervals for the decline. Without time-correlated model draws, the uncertainty of a peak year, change statistic, or regression slope cannot be estimated reliably from annual bounds alone.

knitr::kable(endpoint_bounds |> select(country,source,stress_smallest_pct,
                                      stress_largest_pct,stress_sign_stable),
             digits=1, caption='Illustrative endpoint-bound sensitivity (not a confidence interval)')
Illustrative endpoint-bound sensitivity (not a confidence interval)
country source stress_smallest_pct stress_largest_pct stress_sign_stable
Kenya UNAIDS -86.8 -72.7 Decline across endpoints
South Africa UNAIDS -76.8 -8.6 Decline across endpoints
Uganda UNAIDS -53.1 -15.3 Decline across endpoints
Kenya IHME -71.0 -45.8 Decline across endpoints
South Africa IHME -76.2 -51.6 Decline across endpoints
Uganda IHME -85.1 -8.9 Decline across endpoints

Interpretation to complete after running the analysis: Explain whether both sources support the same direction of progress, whether country rankings change, and whether the endpoint stress test changes the qualitative interpretation. Any differences may reflect estimation methods, underlying evidence, rounding, or uncertainty. They do not establish causality or identify the correct source.

AI-assisted code validation

I also evaluated an AI-generated R approach for calculating percentage change between 1990 and 2024. My first synthetic test included duplicate observations for one country-year. The original reshaping approach retained an observation-count column, which could split one country into multiple rows. I revised the workflow to keep diagnostic counts separate from the values being reshaped and tested missing baselines, zero baselines, duplicate observations, and a missing baseline year.

The synthetic tests are in ai_validation.R. They are separate from the real epidemiological analyses because I intentionally created edge cases that should not be assumed to occur in the OWID source files. I recorded the AI assistance and checked the expected outputs independently.

source('ai_validation.R')

Limitations and next steps

The main limitations are ecological inference, estimated rather than observed infection totals, possible differences between source definitions, unequal data availability across indicators, and the use of absolute pediatric infection counts rather than a validated mother-to-child transmission rate. Country and year adjustments do not eliminate confounding. I would not use these results to make clinical recommendations.

A next step would be to obtain joint uncertainty draws, population or birth denominators, and additional prevention indicators where the definitions and coverage are compatible. The companion Shiny app allows users to explore the descriptive results and see how many observations contribute to each view.

Data sources and reproducibility

  • Our World in Data HIV/AIDS topic page: https://ourworldindata.org/hiv-aids
  • Underlying source estimates: UNAIDS and IHME; exact indicator URLs, access dates, units, and licenses should be entered in data/SOURCES.md before publishing.
  • Run analysis.R to regenerate figures and tables. Run ai_validation.R to check synthetic cases. Run app.R to launch the dashboard.
